title: Special Report: My So-Called Alpha School
author: Build Cognitive Resonance
summary: This special report investigates Alpha School's high school 'boot camp,' the first eight weeks of the school year, using an extensive review of 40-plus verified student Twitter accounts that the school itself promoted, to document a set of practices including required public Twitter posting toward 100 followers, biometric heart-rate monitoring while watching recorded parental critique videos, unpaid labor cleaning restaurant kitchens and gas-station bathrooms recorded on audio, and a self-directed 'discovery learning' requirement to complete an AP unit and score a 5 on its exam within five days using AI. The report highlights a specific documented contradiction: Alpha School's own consultant, Carl Hendrick, has publicly and repeatedly criticized discovery learning as pedagogically unsound, yet the school's flagship activity is built entirely on unsupervised discovery learning. Business-oriented curriculum content (Radical Candor, Extreme Ownership, a Harvard Everest simulation) dominates the reviewed material, with the author noting zero references to any work of fiction across more than 40 student accounts and hundreds of tweets. Reactions collected from named educators and an EdTech-law attorney span from concerns about student wellbeing and safeguarding to characterizing the school's core value proposition as marketing rather than substantiated pedagogy, while Alpha School's PR representative declined a point-by-point response and called the characterizations false. The author, after independently investigating whether the accounts might be inauthentic PR-generated content, concludes the accounts and their activities are genuine, and frames the report as a call for further journalistic scrutiny of student experience at the school.
points: Documents a specific, verifiable contradiction: Alpha School's own paid consultant, Carl Hendrick, has publicly criticized discovery learning in his own published work, while the school's central boot-camp activity requires students to master an entire AP exam unit through unsupervised discovery learning in five days.

Grounds the investigation in primary evidence, over 40 school-promoted student Twitter accounts and hundreds of tweets, rather than secondhand claims, and explicitly investigated and ruled out the possibility the accounts were inauthentic before publishing.

Surfaces the specific mechanics of biometric monitoring (heart rate held within 10% of baseline while watching recorded parental critique in front of classmates) as a concrete, sourced practice rather than a vague characterization of surveillance.

Notes the near-total absence of fiction across the entire reviewed corpus of student accounts, using that absence as indirect evidence of the curriculum's exclusively business- and metrics-oriented orientation.

Collects on-record reactions from named educators and an EdTech-law attorney spanning safeguarding concern, marketing-versus-pedagogy skepticism, and outright dismissal, rather than relying solely on the author's own interpretation.
quotes: As part of boot camp, they are required to post on Twitter and obtain at least 100 followers.

Alpha School students apparently have their heart rates monitored as they watch recorded videos of their parents critiquing them, in front of their classmates, and students must keep their heart rates within 10 percent of their baseline to pass.

During boot camp, Alpha School students apparently engage in sustained discovery learning, described by some students as a core life skill: they must complete one unit of an Advanced Placement course and receive a score of 5 on the end-of-unit exam within five days, entirely through their own self-directed learning using AI and the internet.

Hendrick is a longtime vocal critic of discovery learning, having co-authored a book with chapters titled Why independent learning is not a good way to become an independent learner and Why discovery learning is a bad way to discover things.

Schooling fulfills the function of accountability. In the future, this will mean cameras on, and an AI monitoring student behavior, their latency, what websites they are looking at, their ability to focus and then producing a report for a human tutor.
In reviewing more than 40 students' accounts and hundreds of tweets, I did not see a single reference to a work of fiction.
The real talent of folks at Alpha School is marketing. Their marketing is full of high-level claims about what is possible in education and very few details about exactly why what they do works.
What's happening at Alpha School should shock the conscience, and going forward, everyone who covers them should ask hard questions about the student experience at Alpha School as described here.
